subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIEW OF FIREARMS CONTROL PROVISIONS
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs be authorized to review the firearms control provisions, sections 82 to 106 inclusive of the Criminal Code of Canada, and that such review extend to all aspects of the firearms control program and include the hearing and consideration of the views of the interested persons and organizations and to make recommendations with respect to any amendments, alterations or modifications thereto that appear to the committee then to be necessary or desirable;
That the committee have power to adjourn from place to place within Canada; and
That the committee be empowered to retain the services of expert advisers and to commission studies or research to assist in its work and that it also be empowered to retain such professional, technical, clerical and stenographic help as may be required.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this private member's motion standing in my name in essence asks that this House authorize a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs to investigate, hear briefs, cross the country and employ counsel and advisers respecting the legislation commonly known as gun control legislation which is now part of the Criminal Code. 1 think it is essential that we now do this. I think the time is ripe for this Parliament and, as a matter of fact, this government, to find this an ideal vehicle to plumb the many questions which exist with respect to the administration of our gun control legislation.
Second, this would be an ideal vehicle for taking a very hard and searching look at the whole philosophy and concept of our gun control legislation and, obviously and most important, to
February 2, 1981

figure out now, after three years of operation, whether it is achieving its purpose.
I think a little history is called for. In August of 1977 Parliament approved very comprehensive revisions to the gun control provisions of the Criminal Code. It was at that time and continues to this day to be one of the most sensitive issues to come before Parliament in recent years. It certainly is in the whole law and order field, in any event.
Hon. members should know that very large numbers of citizens of Canada are very directly affected by this legislation. There are more than three million gun owners in Canada, and gun owners and, I suggest, certainly non-gun owners alike are vitally concerned about the level of violence in our society which is related to guns and the use of guns.
The key provisions of the 1977 legislation established a system which required any person over 16 years of age who wished to acquire-by purchase, by borrowing or by trading- a firearm, to obtain a firearms acquisition certificate, commonly known as an FAC. A screening system was established to identify those with criminal or violent records and, obviously, a system then to deny firearms acquisition certificates to those people. That is the principle and the theory. In practice, of course, I feel-and I would like to hear some rebuttal-that that system has not worked and is not working, simply because those with that type of record or history are not stopped by this system. I am not talking about the spontaneous marital difficulty in which somebody reaches into a cupboard for a shotgun or a .22 to settle an argument by that means; I am talking about those who have histories of violent criminal activity or those with histories of using guns during crime. I suggest that in practice those latter people are the very people it does not affect, although it is supposed to in theory. If it does not affect those people, it does not affect anybody because it cannot possibly affect those whose spontaneous reaction to an argument is to reach for a gun for which they may already have a certificate.
The system simply does not work against those who have that record of criminal activity solely and simply because they circumvent the system by paying no attention to it. They ignore it. If someone is going to rob a bank with a gun, I suggest that he does not run down to his friendly local police station to get an FAC ahead of time.
Under the FAC system an individual does not need a certificate in order to possess any gun he acquired before 1979. I suggest that this is a very glaring practical gap in the legislation facing the police today. How do they know, for instance, when a person acquired an older gun? I suggest that most of the guns in use in Canada today were acquired long before 1979.
To assist the police in solving some of the problems they have-and they are very grave and gross problems-the police were given almost unprecedented wide powers to search for and seize weapons without warrant. I suggest that this has been criticized very severely in many civil rights, legal and justice quarters of this country. It is an unprecedented provision to write into legislation such as this, and I suggest that
Firearms Control
this is another area of scope which should be looked at very closely by means of an inquiry.
The administration of the whole firearms acquisition certificate system was turned over by the federal government to the provinces. Most provinces issue FACs from local police offices, with the notable exception of New Brunswick where all such certificates are issued from a central processing office, so therefore the main bulk of the administration-as far as the public perception is concerned in any event-falls on the shoulders of local police officers in local offices.
We all know that the enforcement of the Criminal Code itself is a provincial responsibility. However, due to the rather unusual administrative requirements of the firearms provisions, and especially the whole system of issuing firearms acquisition certificates and issuing business permits, the federal government of the day entered into a federal-provincial agreement-into many federal-provincial agreements, actually-whereby deficits incurred by the provinces will be paid by the federal government. As far as I can ascertain, there has not been a report since 1977 respecting the amount of moneys required in respect of this whole system. How much has been spent, for instance, by municipal police forces across this country in respect of firearms acquisition certificates and their administration? How much has been spent by provincial forces or out of provincial treasuries? We have never really received a report on how much the federal government has spent in total in respect of this whole system.
We have never been told which provinces have deficits and how much of a deficit they have incurred. I suggest to you, sir, that that information is available to the government, that it should be released, and that it should be released to a parliamentary inquiry.
In 1977, and again in 1979, it was estimated by the federal officials in the Department of the Solicitor General that a total of 600,000 to 700,000 FACs would be issued annually. Since this program has been in effect we have only had two reports to the solicitors general which show a significantly lower number than the number announced. In its first year, for instance, only 245,000 certificates were issued, not the 600,000 or 700,000 which we have been led to believe would be the number. Why the difference? What has happened? Were the first estimates-the only estimates we have had-that far out, or has there been that much of a decline in the acquisition of new weapons in this country?
What are the 1980 figures? The minister must have them by now. 1 hope that the parliamentary secretary, who, I would assume, will speak in this debate, has those figures and will give them to us. However, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you that they are far out of line with the original estimates which were given to the House in 1977 when the legislation was passed. Either something has happened in the meantime, or it is the effect of the legislation, although I do not think so. Obviously that legislation was passed by the House with the misleading information to show that it was that much of a problem and

February 2, 1981
Firearms Control
that there were that many weapons traded each year since that time.
In 1979, for instance, there was a six months' backlog in the processing of applications to acquire firearm acquisition certificates. Presumably these have been cleared up, but a veil of secrecy has been drawn and a great deal of non-information has been coming out of the Department of the Solicitor General with respect to the time it now takes to obtain the certificates. I ask whoever will be replying for the government today how long a person has to wait for a certificate to be issued to him, provided he has no criminal record or no record of violent disorders. The National Advisory Council on Firearms was asked by the Department of the Solicitor General to provide independent advice on the program to the government. Is it still in existence, and where are the reports? Why have we not heard the concerns of this group? A veil of secrecy has been drawn over the whole matter of gun control registration in the last little while, and it is time that many of these concerns were answered.
I suspect that there is a great number of problems regarding administration, and I suspect that there is a great number of suggested amendments to the legislation which are ready to be processed through the House. Yet we have heard absolutely nothing about them. By the middle of 1979, without any of the confirming statistics which have since become available to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), 13 amendments to the legislation were identified as being needed. Here we are well into 1981 and nothing has been forthcoming, no statement, no statistics. For instance, some of the amendments identified well over a year and a half ago included such matters as safety training requirements under the act. Surely if we are going to be burdened with this type of legislation there should be an objective in view with regard to the acquisition of new weapons in this country by individuals, and some requirements with regard to safety training. This whole aspect has been ignored by the government. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that amendments with respect to that aspect have been ready for some time now.
Another real problem has been the whole matter relating to security firms in this country. An FAC is issued to an individual, not to a company. Most security firms require the ownership and use of a weapon, which is unfortunate, in my view. It is not possible, as has been suggested to this government by provincial governments, for some type of a blanket permit to be issued to these security firms?
Customs tariff amendments have been ready for some time as they relate to the importation into this country of firearms by Canadian citizens, but absolutely nothing has been brought forward regarding this by the government. Then there is the matter of dealing with non-residents who attempt to import weapons temporarily into this country without an FAC. This matter has not been tackled at all. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very real and continuing problem to the tourist industry in this country in so far as American hunters are concerned. No matter who is involved, a certificate is required in this country for anyone carrying a gun.
What do Americans do who bring guns across the border temporarily? Do they apply for an FAC? If they apply for an FAC, do the police forces in the country check their medical records or their violent tendencies, if any? I suggest that a double standard is being applied with regard to Americans who come in and Canadian citizens. 1 am not even sure that the government is enforcing these provisions of the act. All this is a can of worms. If it did enforce them, there would be a great anguished outcry from the tourist outfitters and from the whole tourist industry in the country. In many ways the government has shut its eyes with regard to the problem of non-residents who bring their weapons into this country temporarily for a lawful purpose.
Then there is the whole question of appeals, another matter which has to be dealt with. There is simply no appeal provision in the act at the moment with regard to those who are denied a free firearm acquisition certificate. There are other questions and other procedural problems in respect of the legislation regarding appeals. That is another area which should be considered very carefully by a parliamentary committee, I suggest. More problems have surfaced now since the first phase of that legislation was proclaimed on January 1, 1978.
The time for a complete review of the administration of the act is now long overdue and should be dealt with as promptly as possible. The proper body to deal with it is a parliamentary committee. The whole purpose of the legislation, the whole philosophy and the whole concept behind it, are to reduce the number of crimes committed with guns in Canada, and after two full years since the legislation was passed a valid question should be asked by all of us. The question is whether this legislation is achieving that purpose. I must say to you, sir, that I have grave doubts that it is. It seems to me to be a cumbersome, awkward, and expensive system. But I would like to know for sure. I would like to learn from those who must enforce it and from those who have a very expert and detailed knowledge of it.
The first two annual firearms reports-the only ones we have ever received-for 1977 and 1978 do not reveal any evident trend toward a sharp reduction in the violent crime rate. The statistics for early 1980, which we now have, show that violent crime, crime connected to guns, is on the upsurge in this country. Just last week the report of the Metropolitan Toronto Police Commission for 1980 was released. For instance, in metro-Toronto alone crime is up 9.4 per cent, most of which is violent crime. In the city of Toronto during 1980 ten citizens were killed during acts of robbery, compared to only one in 1979. Out of a total of 48 homicides last year in metro-Toronto, 18 people were shot to death. Robberies with firearms increased 23 per cent in metro-Toronto in 1980-386 in 1980 compared to 289 in 1979.
I end by saying this to you, Mr. Speaker. The Trudeau government in 1979 made a public commitment to carry out a review of the firearms control provisions of the Criminal Code. It was never done by the previous Liberal administration. The
February 2, 1981

Clark government confirmed that commitment and, as solicitor general in that government, I publicly stated that it would be done. At that time 1 put on the Order Paper the very same motion which I put forward today. Some of the most pertinent statistics relating to violent crimes in this country have been hidden from view. But they are available. There is no need for further time to draw conclusions. 1 think it is time now for a parliamentary review by a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. This would permit the provinces, the federal officials, the RCMP, individual groups and individuals, to present briefs and comment on legislation which, I suspect, is not working. Most of all, sir, that inquiry would be open and available to us all.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Small Businesses)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIEW OF FIREARMS CONTROL PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity today to speak on this motion of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence). I must suggest that perhaps, like all existing legislation, it has to be updated from time to time.
I believe that the implementation of Bill C-51 in 1977 was a very big step to take. Perhaps people, hunters and gun owners particularly, were of the opinion it went too far. The passage of that legislation was certainly marked by some controversy. The successful though controversial amnesty recall program took place in November, 1978. Then the introduction of the firearm acquisition certificates and the business permit systems took effect on January 1, 1979. It must be noted, however, that the recall was regarded as very successful, if you talk to various police officers. The rank and file of law-abiding citizens were not affected by it.
As significant as those changes were, I think they should be reviewed in the context of the history of firearms control in Canada. It is now widely appreciated that Canadian law has controlled firearms in one manner or another for well over 100 years. 1 well remember during the Second World War when all firearms had to be registered. You had to sign to buy ammunition. The first permit system for the carrying of a small arm outside of one's residence or place of business was introduced in 1882. By 1934 the law required the registration of all hand guns. A change in the law in 1968 created three classes of weapons in Canada: prohibited, restricted, and unrestricted.
I bring this brief history to the attention of the House because I believe it sheds some light on why Canada has generally enjoyed a history of responsible use of firearms since we have advanced from a frontier society, which to a large extent depended on firearms. The conditions in Canada are a far cry from what we see in other countries around us at this time. The changes enacted by Parliament in 1977 continued the promotion of the responsible use of firearms, in the Canadian tradition. The one big change which was effected was the firearm acquisition certificate.
As I mentioned, the 1968 law created three classes of weapons: prohibited, restricted, and unrestricted. The condi-
Firearms Control
tions attached by that legislation affected the acquisition and use of restricted guns. There were no controls imposed on the acquisition of either long arms such as shotguns or hunting rifles. The criminal law amendment legislation in 1977 introduced control of long arms to the extent of requiring individuals wishing to acquire them to be screened by the police to ensure that they did not have a criminal record or a history of mental illness associated with violence.
I received a letter recently from a constituent of mine. She is now a married lady, and she spoke about this matter. She related to me an experience she had with a friend, her married brother and her sister-in-law one evening. A man, such as I referred to previously, with a history of mental illness, shot her friend when in the car with the rest of them. It is a tragedy she will never forget. This is the type of instance to which this regulation was intended to apply, not to the normal rank and file person who likes to hunt.
I like to hunt, on occasion. I was not affected by this legislation. Perhaps, in a sense, there is a reason why I was not affected. My first experience as a hunter, as one who loves the outdoors, was not just with the sport of hunting but the need for predatory control of the foxes which were wantonly destroying the poultry in our area. We used to raise those birds on the range. A few years after that we had a rabies epidemic. The hunters in the area would organize a fox drive in order to eradicate the foxes and this problem. A few years ago two of my employees had to go through a series of vaccination shots for rabies. Not long afterwards we all became very conscious of the need for organized hunters and the help they provided to the farmers and society while we were constantly trying to rid the countryside of those animals which do carry rabies.
There is another area to which this also applies. In mid-November we had a baby calf killed in pasture by a brush wolf. Naturally, the cow, on mother's instinct, hid the calf away during the daylight hours and she would return to it in the morning and the evening to feed it. One night we heard her bawling. We went to find her and we discovered the baby calf dead. So there is a need for the farmer and the hunter to have weapons available to them. This is certainly not restricted, in a sense. But if there is a backlog of people waiting for acquisition certificates I hope it will be resolved.
Another reason why I am interested in this legislation is because, when I was a teenager, just after World War II, I was involved in a fox hunt in which a friend of mine accidentally shot himself. It was a tragedy in the community which left a wife and three children. The real tragedy was that this man was a war veteran. He had been all through World War II and many battles. Then, as the result of one little accident, his life was ended. That shocking incident made me volunteer to become an instructor in the use of firearms. I wanted to see that the young people of my area were properly instructed in the use of firearms. Yet, this war veteran who had handled firearms during the battles of the war had his life stamped out by one simple mistake.

February 2, 1981
Firearms Control
Another area about which I am concerned is the safe storage of firearms and ammunition. Part of the program of instruction dealt with the prime concern that every owner keep firearms out of the reach of children, by keeping the guns locked up in a place separate from the ammunition. I understand the concern of the hon. member who introduced this bill. According to his interpretation of the law, if somebody's home was broken into and the guns and ammunition removed, that person can be held responsible.
There was a case just a few weeks ago in which a policeman was shot and killed. The suspected individuals were apprehended near Orillia, after a trail of crime with ultimate tragic results which began near North Bay. I do not know whether the involved weapons had been properly stored, or the premises in which they were kept were forcibly entered. I suggest a review of this case could indicate necessary amendments or changes to relieve these problems. We should also review the matter from the standpoint that a break and enter occurred.
An area of concern to many hunters, particularly those in my area, is the right of the police to search and seize if they have reason to believe that the situation is dangerous. I understand the feelings of the policemen who must enter a tense situation, whether domestic or otherwise. The police are empowered to search for and seize guns in emotionally-charged situations of conflict. It enables them to deal effectively with the kind of situation which leads to almost two-thirds of the deaths caused by firearms each year in Canada. The intent of the legislation was to ensure that officers exercising such authority would explain to a court why it was impractical to obtain a search warrant in advance.
I understand the feelings of people who might be subject to search and seizure. I hope in the review which is under way that this particular section will be examined in detail, in order that it does not infringe upon the rights of normal law-abiding citizens. No doubt there are arguments for and against this point. I can understand the situation where a policeman is called to a crime as the result of some domestic dispute. Such an incident occurred this Christmas in my own village. A neighbour had visited another neighbour. I am not sure whether it was an emotional disturbance or whether it arose as a result of a celebration. The neighbour demanded a gun and was refused. The wife ran next door to call the police. In the meantime the fellow got a heavy rifle. When the unsuspecting police knocked on the door, it was opened and the neighbour fired. Luckily the police were not hurt, but an innocent bystander was injured.
I understand why legislators feel there must be an element of protection for persons who may be emotionally disturbed. The individual to which I just referred would never have considered doing such a thing under normal circumstances. Even though he went to another home to obtain a weapon, an innocent bystander was hurt.
I hope the evaluation being conducted by the Department of the Solicitor General considers such situations and will employ
more acceptable and better-understood solutions for people in Canada who own weapons. I understand the study is examining the effects of the firearms provisions of the Criminal Code and that it is not merely confined to changes to the law passed in 1977. The review promised by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), following the completion of the evaluation study in 1982, will affect the review of the entire history of firearms control in Canada.
This study is a very important first step in the review. I hope to play a part in any further review and to reflect, as a Member of Parliament, the wishes of my constituents, taking into consideration the part played by law enforcement officers, average citizens, hunters, land and property owners. While I appreciate the strong interest of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland on this subject, I hope he understands the review would not be as useful as it would with the results of the study at hand. The time to make a decision on whether we should proceed with a review is when the evaluation study is made public.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this matter, but I have the sinking feeling that for some reason-and 1 do not wish to be accusatory-government members intend to talk this bill out. Frankly, I find that very disturbing; I might even be so naive as to say that I find it rather surprising. I compliment the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) on introducing the bill. 1 believe that a review is necessary. This bill is consistent with the measure put on the order paper by the hon. member when he was solicitor general. At the time there was not a peep of complaint from the opposition party of the day.
If I understand the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson), the review is premature in light of the ongoing study in the Department of the Solicitor General. I do not wish to criticize public servants in that department who are allegedly conducting this study because I do not know what they are doing or whether they received direct instruction from the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) to do a complete and expeditious study of the legislation under the Criminal Code as it affects gun control. I have no idea, and I will likely never find out.
However, rather than use this as an excuse to postpone a review, I would far sooner compare this situation to a similar motion which dealt with Canadian penitentiaries. Had we waited for the Department of the Solicitor General to conduct a review of the penitentiaries, we would all be serving life terms because it would never come. At that time a Liberal government was in power, so I am not being partisan.
At that time we were able to prevail upon the then solicitor general to say, "We have a Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, so let us give it a House order which will enable it to establish a subcommittee. Let it travel, let it call expert witnesses, and let it have the necessary staff."
February 2, 1981

Those of us who were exposed to that process said to ourselves at the completion of it, "This is the way the House of Commons and parliamentarians should work." We did not say that as Liberals, as Conservatives or as members of the NDP, we said it as parliamentarians.
At that time I detected a great lift in the morale of parliamentarians because they were part of a process that was not partisan. They travelled night and day and worked night and day in not too attractive surroundings and in an atmosphere not too conducive to morale, that of the Canadian penitentiaries.
I thought the report that was produced was an outstanding piece of parliamentary work. My friends opposite were members of that committee and there was a member of the NDP, a bitter political foe, Stu Leggatt, who now serves in the British Columbia legislature, who virtually put his heart into the report.
I have a terrible feeling now that there is some resistance over there-for what reason I do not know-to permitting a good and viable institution, a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, to fulfil a mandate not to criticize, not to change the legislation, but to review it.
We have all been the recipients of complaints about this legislation. I am concerned when I hear of the number of violent deaths increasing in metropolitan Toronto because the same might happen in my home town of Stratford. I have not yet seen the report of our police force for 1980.
I am sure my colleague, the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham is not one to say, as I am not, that this is all bad or this is all good. He said that we should create a vehicle in which parliamentarians could work together diligently and effectively to review this legislation. The operative word-and it was used twice-is "reviews"; not to change, not to amend, not to abrogate, but to review.
We all enjoy partisan politics-I as much as anyone-but surely in the context of having the president of the penitentiary committee before us, the government will not be so inflexible and dogmatic as to prevent that vehicle from instituting what I am sure hon. members on all sides feel is a very worth while project for parliamentarians and not necessarily only for public servants.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIEW OF FIREARMS CONTROL PROVISIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REVIEW OF FIREARMS CONTROL PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in this discussion, and I welcome the initiative of the hon. member opposite in raising this matter again.
When Bill C-51 was introduced in 1977, it was necessarily controversial and there were strong differences of opinion between those who wanted more rigorous gun controls and those who wanted fewer or no controls. In my constituency at that time people were very exercised because of a murder which had been committed by a person who was obviously mentally disturbed. He was able to buy a gun without question, took that gun and shot some innocent passersby. I
Firearms Control
remember very vividly the strength of the convictions and the views of those who felt that there surely was a case for making it extremely difficult for people to obtain guns.
At the same time, a colleague from British Columbia received a letter from a farm wife who was very worried in case the government made it too difficult for people to buy and store guns. This farmer wrote about a situation where a wolf had come on her property and she was able to save her child's life, only because she had immediate access to a loaded gun.
These regional differences had to be reconciled at that time and because there was no way to reach a solution which would be satisfactory to everyone, the government undertook to continue reviewing and evaluating the program.
A three-year evaluation and study is now being done under the aegis of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) by a consultant firm in co-operation with the provinces. I understand it is a very broad study which will examine all firearms provisions in the Criminal Code, not only the amendments put in place by Bill C-51.
The final report will be available in 1982 but there will be two interim reports. I suppose the question before us today is whether the reference to the standing committee recommended by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) is more useful if done now or when at least the interim report is available.
Those of us who were dealing with Bill C-81 in many cases found ourselves somewhat handicapped by lack of statistics. For instance, Statistics Canada did not start collecting data on a regular basis on the use of firearms in connection with crime in general until 1974, even though there were useful figures available before that on homicides involving firearms.
Although Bill C-51 was introduced in 1977, the changes to the restricted weapons system came into force on January 1, 1978, the amnesty recall program was in November, 1978, and the firearms acquisition certificate and business permits system took effect on January 1, 1979. In effect, if there were a reference to the standing committee at this point, we would be dealing with the experience of two years and would be without the benefit of the interim report on the study.
As the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) pointed out, Canadian law has controlled firearms in one manner or another for more than 100 years. This is something which seems to be lost sight of because many people think that Bill C-81 was the beginning of firearms control in Canada. The first permit system for carrying a small arm outside one's residence or place of business was introduced in 1892, and by 1934 the law required the registration of all handguns. Controls on long guns had to wait for the 1977-78 amendments, although there were some changes in 1968.
Canada is fortunate in having had control of possession and use of small guns for the past 50 years, and it is important that these controls be maintained. The low handgun ownership rate probably accounts for the relatively low rate of homicide by handguns. If handguns are not readily available they cannot be stolen, misused, accidentally used or used for suicide; and

February 2, 1981
Firearms Control
suicide has to concern us as much as the use of handguns in murders, whether criminel murders or family murders.
If the level of ownership of handguns is very low, citizens will not feel they have to acquire them for protection. We have seen the unfortunate situation in the United States where law-abiding citizens feel that they have to own handguns for protection. In some cases, those guns are used against them by robbers.
Long guns, however, are now playing a significant part in homicides. It is reckoned that about one-third of homicides in Canada are committed with long guns. The new controls instituted in 1977 do at least provide us with a more effective way of limiting the number of those homicides. Perhaps it is particularly important to be concerned about long guns because they can be sawn off and used as handguns. Sometimes the ammunition for long guns is interchangeable with other types of ammunition. Controls tend to emphasize that any type of gun is dangerous and must be handled with care. This is not to impose unnecessary restriction on sportsmen who use their guns responsibly. In fact, much of the public's education on the use of guns has been initiated by sportmen's associations. One program in particular, organized by the province of Ontario in conjunction with sportmen's associations, is considered to have had important effects in reducing accidental deaths and injuries from the use of long guns.
As the member opposite pointed out, many people are concerned about the human rights implications of the present law. Of course, this is always a very difficult judgment call to make. The law gives police authority to search for guns in certain cases of domestic disputes when they have reason to fear a person is out of control and may be in possession of a gun. An officer who uses this authority is required to make a return to a court explaining why it was not practical to obtain a search warrant in advance. Needless to say, we would not want to see any further erosion of the principle that one's home is a place where a person is entitled to privacy. On the other hand, if an officer's action prevents a murder or a suicide, there would be a very grateful family.
Two-thirds of all killings by firearms in Canada still occur as a result of family disputes or so-called crimes of passion. These are dangerous situations, emotionally charged usually as a result of an issue between people who know each other well.
The question of suicide also arises in many of these cases. I agree it is a difficult judgment call for the officer. If one can find some better way of not only ensuring the protection of people's privacy, but also protection of human life, perhaps we should look at this again.
The question of safety continues to be an important one. When citizens become concerned about gun laws, they think primarily of guns being used by criminals in the course of other crimes. The last figure I have been able to find for that shows that about 7 per cent of killings as a result of gun use occur in the context of other crimes.
The amendments to Bill C-81 provided for the courts to impose sentences in the case of people in possession of a gun while committing another crime. The courts do seem to be using this provision which provides for punishment after the crime, but of course does not deal with the more important question of preventing such crimes.
Firearms acquisition certificates are considered generally to be reasonably hard to obtain in the sense that they cannot be obtained by a person on impulse. Evidence of character must be provided. However, criminals will always have their own sources in one way or another to obtain firearms. I am not sure that one can provide legislation to prevent any and every illegal act. It does seem as though the amendments which have been put in place by Bill C-81 up to now have provided us with improved controls and as well some useful mechanisms for their continuation.
