speechtext:
The House again in Committee of the Whole for the study of Bill C-54, to amend the statute law relating to income tax.

When the committee rose at five o'clock, clause 1 of the bill was under consideration. The hon. member for Fundy-Royal had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, at five o'clock I was concluding my remarks with regard to the potential of the oil shale and natural gas fields in Albert county of New Brunswick. I was explaining how unfortunate it was that exploration investment money was being driven out of this country by the policies of the government. I had asked the minister to reexamine the policies to comply with the requests of provincial authorities, as well as those 1 have made at various times in this House, and to give some thought to exploring, and possibly exploiting, potential oil in the province of New Brunswick.
Income Tax Act
I wish to deal with an extraordinary group of people throughout this country. They form a substantially small group compared to the manufacturers and others with lobby groups that are heard. This group of individuals is critical to the nation. They farm the land and grow the food to feed Canadians.
This group is facing undue hardships. Interest rates are rising, apparently uncontrolled. The government has demonstrated a lack of interest in the problems they face. They must deal with rising fuel costs, labour problems and other hardships. They should be given special consideration.
If interest rates cannot be controlled, some consideration should be given to the difficulties in which they find themselves. They are experiencing dwindling profits, if any at all. We will be in dire straits if this group of very valuable individuals, the small farmers of the country, is no longer able to carry on because of the financial difficulties it is experiencing.
Assistance could be given in a way such as was suggested by the previous government. I refer to capital gains considerations, a matter which has been raised on several occasions by my colleagues. Members of the party to my left made reference to certain individuals in this party who are in favour of abolishing capital gains. I would classify myself as one of those. It is true that those who have money are able to make more money out of circumstances such as that. However, what is wrong with a climate where people with money are prepared to invest it at home so that other people can work, feed their families and enjoy all of the good things which this country should be able to provide for them? Unfortunately, what we have in the mini-budget and budget is a conglomeration of political wing-dingery which will not come to grips with the problems facing the nation. This nation has the greatest potential of any on the face of the earth. However, we find ourselves in dire circumstances with a very bleak future. There must be a change in rationale.
I ask the minister to re-examine these policies which are driving this country down the path of economic and social chaos, policies formed over the past number of years and still fostered by the government. We need new and innovative policies to lead us out of this dead end street which can only lead to economic and social collapse.

Mr. Chairman, as this is the second opportunity I have had to speak on clause 1 of Bill C-54, I will be fairly brief. There are a few matters I want to place on record prior to the in-depth clause by clause study of this legislation. I want to review with the committee a couple of motions under Standing Order 43 which I had the pleasure to move and to make some representations in the hope that the government will take action in these areas. It is obvious there is a great deal of concern among all Canadians over the inaction of our friends opposite. We find in reality that the budgetary proposals they have brought forward will do very little for many sectors of our society. This government has set a number of records in its term of office; a number of records of which it

February 2, 1981
Income Tax Act
should not be very proud and a number of records it should bring forward legislation to counteract.
When we view the record of this government, we find under this administration we have record high interest rates, record high government spending, record high budgetary deficits, record high unemployment, record high taxation, record high inflation, and our dollar is at its lowest level in years. It is for that reason I moved my motion today.
We note from the reports brought forward by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that a record number of individual enterprises, businesses, individuals and corporations are facing bankruptcy in Canada. The figures that department has come forward with show that over-all bankruptcies in Canada were up some 17.3 per cent in 1980 as compared to 1979. As far as individuals are concerned, bankruptcies are up some 23.4 per cent, and business failures are up some 28.9 per cent from a year earlier. It is because of the inaction of this Liberal administration that so many sectors of our society are facing the difficulties they are facing today.
We brought forward a number of initiatives in the budget we presented when in government, and I am happy to see that a number of those initiatives have been accepted and were included in the budget recently brought down by the Minister of Finance.
There is one segment of our society which may be more notable than others on fixed incomes facing severe problems and difficulties, that is, the single parent sector. That sector accounts for approximately 9 per cent of our family population, and about 50 per cent of these individuals who are single parents have income levels below the poverty line. I should hope the government would give some special consideration to these individuals facing so many difficulties.
An hon. member of the New Democratic Party on Friday- and I cannot recall the specific individual's constituency- brought forward a motion pertaining to this very important problem. Hon. members came forward with a number of suggestions as to how we might help these individuals, not only in the area of taxation, but in the area of other legislation which pertains to them.
It is obvious when we note the actions of the minister responsible for the status of women, that callous attitude with which he treated the status of women group, he does not have any specific or sincere concern for them.
I hope the government will adopt a number of the recommendations these very valuable groups have come forward with, not only in respect of taxation measures, but in respect of other measures which affect single-parent families.
Coming from western Canada I should like to put on record some of the grievances individuals have in that area. While some of the topics I will touch upon do not directly deal with the legislation before us, I hope to connect those remarks to the clauses that pertain to this legislation.
The prairie region has fought long and bitterly against the colonial conditions imposed upon it by the populous and politically powerful region of central Canada. If forced to fight again it will. Today it is absolutely convinced that the tax policies of our Minister of Finance and the energy plans of our minister responsible for energy imply a reversion to the west's old colonial status. The west will not resume the role of a colony without resistance.
We not only have the budgetary measures as they pertain to energy, we also have the constitutional proposals which in essence make us in the western provinces, in fact all those provinces outside Quebec and Ontario, second-class citizens.
Let me just go back into a bit of the history. Historically the political and commercial powers of the centre have always merged their interests; the management of the resources of western Canada for the benefit of the central commercial empire of Canada was and is their principal joint venture. The mutual benefit from the merger was control of the resources of the prairies for the commercial benefit of the industries of the centre and the concurrence electoral support for industry's political allies in the east where it really counted. Both stood to win. The fact that the west stood to lose was a regrettable side effect that resulted from the nature of the nation.
Inescapably the purposes of the dominion and the national interest were and are still defined by the economic and political power blocs of central Canada. In 1867 one of the terms of the confederation of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia was that each province would own and control the natural resources within its borders. In 1870 the region which is now the three prairie provinces was transformed from a trapping and trading preserve of the Hudson's Bay Company and became a colony of the newly-confederated provinces. That same year Manitoba was converted from a colony to a province, but it was not a province like the others. The provinces of Canada owned and controlled their natural resources but Manitoba did neither. Manitoba was really a colony.
In 1905 Alberta and Saskatchewan were carved out of the colonial territories and called provinces but, like Manitoba, they were not permitted to assume ownership and control of their own natural resources. Their resources were retained by Ottawa for the purposes of Canada.
In 1930 anger, agitation, alienation, hostility and periodic talk of separation earned their reward. The ownership and control of natural resources were finally transferred to the prairie provinces. Only in the past 50 years have these provinces been equal partners to the founding partners.
The term "colony" is used carefully. The reality is that the resources of the three provinces were unblushingly used by central Canada for political power and commercial imperialism. For Manitoba's 60 years as a colony it had no adequate real or potential source of provincial revenue. Saskatchewan and Alberta were in a similar state. The three prairie provinces
February 2, 1981

went into the depression and drought of the 1930s in terrible financial situation as a result of the public debt they built up, while Ottawa was looting their land and resources.
Surely viewing history any public policymaker would move with great care. Resource control in the prairie region, as a consequence of past experience, would clearly be viewed as a sensitive and potentially divisive issue. The west has always had to fight the central Canada instinct that western resources belonged to the east. For the long-term interests of Canada that may have been a good policy. Perhaps a strong industrial and commercial heartland was crucial to nation building, but what must be recognized is that, rightly or wrongly, the western provinces see ownership, control and management of resources as their only hope for equity, if they are to sit in on a game which has been Fixed against them. The ability to control these resource is absolutely fundamental to the ability of the three provinces to manage their own economies. In the case of oil and gas, they cannot control price, and this quite evidently weakens their ability to manage their own affairs. If, in addition, a court should find they cannot determine the rate of production'of oil, or any other resource, the prairie provinces joined by British Columbia will revert once again to being colonies of central Canada.
It may be that Ottawa can get a favourable ruling from a court or, through its declaratory powers, can dictate the rate of production of the oil fields of Alberta, but Ottawa would be remarkably foolish if it considered it. What Ottawa needs is not a legal justification but an understanding of the legitimacy of western Canadian concerns.
It would be useful if reason, justice and real understanding of prairie experience could be introduced into the discussions between Alberta and Ottawa. They would be a pleasing substitute for the cleverness of the Ottawa policy planners and for the skilful and cynical massaging of words by the public relations specialists in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
It would be helpful if Ontario came to understand how dangerous western alienation is to Ontario's long-term economic interests. But the real onus is on Ottawa. The real onus is on our friends across the way because Ottawa must learn that sharing, fairness and equity-words so freely used in the National Energy Program-are something more than verbal daggers to wound a debating foe.

Mr. Chairman, when I last spoke about Bill C-54, I had an opportunity to deal with two of the chief deficiencies in this bill and, indeed, two of the chief deficiencies in the act this bill seeks to amend. Those dealt with the general absence of fair play and equity which apply to both taxpayer and Minister of National Revenue alike. 1 also drew attention to the fact that in its present form this bill does nothing to alleviate the absolute inability the average taxpayer of this country, as defined by the act, has in understanding the terms of the act. I suggested at that time that it was the
Income Tax Act
obligation of this House to draft laws which, if they are to be obeyed, are at least to be understood.
The Income Tax Act sought to be amended by Bill C-54 has its legal foundation and justification in Section 91(3) of the British North America Act, which permits the federal gover-ment to impose any tax by any mode or system of taxation, and it refers to the opening paragraph of Section 91 of that act, which grants to the federal government the right to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada.
The Income Tax Act has been used since its predecessor was enacted in September of 1917, originally as a temporary measure, for the purpose of achieving something other than the actual raising of revenues. It has been used for social purposes, and it has been used for the purpose of directing industrial or commercial activities on the part of Canadians. We know that the act has been used in that sense for the purpose of establishing the right of deductions for charitable donations, dependent deductions, and manufacturing and processing incentives. It at one time contained a provision to induce the Canadian public to engage in the very risky business of searching for mines and minerals by providing a tax exempt receipt system which applied to prospectors and those who grubstaked them. Those provisions no longer exist, presumably on the theory that it is no longer necessary to induce people to search actively and take the risks involved in searching for mines and minerals. There was a three-year holiday for mining companies between the time that a mine began to produce minerals in commerical quantities and the time when they became taxable. Similarly, that provision has been eliminated.
I use those illustrations to show that the purpose of the act has not been exclusively to raise revenues but, rather, to direct policies which are in the best interests of the people of Canada.
Accordingly, I come to the major objection to which I should like to draw the attention of the House this evening. My objection is that this bill fails by omission to deal with one of the most essential issues that should confront the government and this House. The bill makes no reference to sections 117 and 123 of the act, which provide the rates of taxation which are to apply to individuals and corporations. Our nation today is beset by high inflationary pressures and by interest rates which are, by their very nature, almost confiscatory in terms of their effect upon the business community in Canada. Because of inflation rates that run in excess of 11 per cent, individuals as employees who have gainful employment will stampede to extract from their employers additional revenues so that they may at least keep pace with the growth of inflation in Canada which the government appears unable to control. An uneasy circumstance will exist which will give rise to industrial disputes and work stoppages, which will have a detrimental effect on our ability as a nation to produce and sell our goods abroad and rectify the imbalance in our international payments.
These circumstances ought to direct the attention of the government to a very simple process, and that process must be the reduction of taxes. Even without current pressures which will be brought upon the Canadian economy it is just and
6800

February 2, 1981
Income Tax Act
reasonable, having regard to internal problems faced by Canadians, that adjustments of a substantial downward nature be made in the rates of tax imposed against Canadian enterprise and Canadian individuals.
The vast amount of tax raised through the Income Tax Act is raised from individuals and not from large corporations or small business corporations in Canada. Of the large amount of taxes raised from individuals, over 70 per cent, according to Revenue Canada's latest statistics, come from employees. If rewarded for their effort by a reduction in the federal government grab, these employees would be in a better position to increase the money supply at their disposal so that they might generate jobs for their fellow Canadians and put a much needed stimulus into the Canadian economy.
The Income Tax Act contains a provision which obliges employers to deduct and remit to Revenue Canada on a regular pay basis that portion of the income tax and Canada Pension Plan contributions which must be made by individual taxpayers who are employees. Without that provision it is doubtful that this country could last one year without a tax revolt. Taxpayers do not realize the immense amount of money they pour into the Treasury or the Consolidated Revenue Fund administered by the Government of Canada. It may be painless to them individually on a weekly, bi-weekly or monthly basis, but the hundreds of millions of dollars which are extracted in this fashion, the billions of dollars which go into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, could best be spent by the people who earn the money, rather than by the government which has shown in the past every inclination to waste it. We could recite illustrations of that for the rest of the evening.
One of the great undertakings of the Prime Minister and of the current government is the creation of an international redistribution of wealth to be carried out under the guise of meeting commitments under the North-South dialogue. This country, through the generosity of its taxpayers who were certainly not consulted about the process, is pumping $1.2 billion annually into foreign aid. We have seen a recent illustration of that in an announcement today that Zimbabwe is to receive $50 million over a period of ten years. That, of course, is but a small illustration of the constant flow of funds from Canada to foreign nations, many of which are under the control of dictatorial regimes which have no respect for the ordinary, generally accepted principles of human dignity. Many of these nations, which operate under a one-party system and therefore might correctly be called dictatorships, have no reference to the democratic system, yet our government persists in the view that it is absolutely essential for us to make these commitments. To what end are we making these commitments?
In 1977 we saw an illustration of the way in which some of these funds were distributed, not directly by CIDA but by another government agency, namely, the Export Development Corporation, measurably assisted by Canadians. It was a loan of some $67 million, as I recall, to Inco which developed a
mine in Guatemala as a result of which the work of miners in the Sudbury area was no longer essential because that company could acquire its raw materials at a cheaper price from Guatemala. What we see here is the citizens of this country paying with their tax dollars to put their fellow citizens out of work. That is exactly how the North-South dialogue will work and how the new international order will work. I think the public should be made well aware of it. Having put their fellow citizens out of work, the public was requested to contribute to the Consolidated Revenue Fund so that unemployment insurance payments may be made to those very people whom they caused to be unemployed.
It is the height of folly; it is something which, as individual donors, very few taxpayers in Canada-certainly no one who used his head-would pursue on an individual basis. I suggest to the government that the people best able to attend to the administration of their funds are the taxpayers of Canada. 1 suggest to the government, if it really believes there is a crying, urgent need expressed by the people of this country to assist others, it let them assist themselves by setting up a machinery whereby donations can flow in from the pocketbooks of those from whom the funds are now extracted by law. They should be asked to make the donations which their government now makes on their behalf.
I made reference to this after commenting upon the provisions of the British North America Act. 1 question the legality of the Government of Canada imposing taxes by any mode or system if it is not for the peace, order and good government of Canada. I recognize that Section 92 in dealing with the right of the provinces to extract direct taxation is confined to the use of those tax funds for purely provincial purposes. The same does not appear in Section 91, but the implication is there.
If we were at the point where we were last year, the issue would not be as significant as it is today. I asked the Minister of Finance in the House on November 17, 1980, the following question:
In light of the change in government which we anticipate in the United States as the result of the recent election there and some of the specific promises by the president-elect to reduce taxation, despite the fact that the minister's budget was recently passed by this House, is it his intention to reduce taxes in Canada in order to correspond with intended tax reductions in the United States, so as to offset the magnet-like effect of attracting business in North America to those jurisdictions with the lowest tax rates?
The minister responded by saying that I was fully aware of the fact that the budget contained a provision for indexing. He might have gone on to say, although he did not, that he promised in his budget the great deductions would be indexed for 1981, but there was no promise for any future year.
Business is attracted to a climate which welcomes it, and the greatest welcome comes from an area in which that business may be conducted allowing it as much of a profit at the end as possible. Such a country is the United States. They will in fact reduce taxes across the board for individuals and for corporations, while our government stands still and does nothing. We need the enterprise and the investment of Canadians. Business must develop in Canada so as to offer jobs, not only to those who do not have them now, but to those who are coming into
February 2, 1981

the work force and who desperately look to this government to lead the way. Instead of creating that climate, the government has turned its back on what is reasonable. It insists upon maintaining a high tax level in Canada so that business expansion will not develop here but will go elsewhere to a place where it is welcome, to a place where jobs will be offered to Americans and not to Canadians. Once the process is begun, it is extremely difficult to retard or reverse it. This government has given no indication that it is even interested in what is going to happen, and yet the handwriting is on the wall.
When Premier Davis journeyed to Japan two years ago, he was met by an observation from the Japanese to the effect that it was pointless to suggest that they invest in Canada because here the rates of taxation were too high for them. We are begging the Japanese to invest in our country; I think that is shameful in itself. We should be investing in our country ourselves, but after the great grab by the federal government, there is little left for anyone to invest. But they told us exactly what their position was. If one examined the foreign aid donations of Japan, one would find they are not as great in terms of their gross national product as are ours.
If one examines the percentage of donations to foreign aid by the United States, one will find that it is markedly less than ours. It is less than half. What has happened is that we are giving our money away so we can go to foreign nations and beg them to invest in our country. The whole situation is crazy. We should be encouraging Canadians to develop their own nation. Why would we ask Japan to come and develop our nation? They have been shrewd enough to look after their own finances well. Is it so that we can then let the dividends and profits from the generation of the business which they might hopefully establish here flow to the United States or Japan?
I earnestly beg the government to look at this issue and to give it the attention it deserves.

Mr. Chairman, I think my remarks tonight will follow very closely the closing peregrinations of the hon. member for York North. Before I get to those remarks, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Mississauga South who very quietly this afternoon, with tremendous knowledge of the detail with which the program works, asked again for the third or fourth time that the government give serious consideration in this bill to the extension of the time allowed for the Small Business Development Bonds. It is only one of the items with which the Crosbie budget tried to reduce taxes on things people needed so that more money would be spent, more jobs would occur and more money would flow back to the taxpayer. It is a very simple request which the member for Mississauga South makes. Even if the government were to extend the expiry date a year he would be grateful. I personally wish they would extend it for at least five years and give small business, whether it be on the farm or in the city, a chance to use development money at about one-half the present interest rate. Within a year or so the government would find that the income flowing back from
Income Tax Act
this program would be much greater than any loss they might suffer.
This is the third time I have spoken with respect to this legislation. I had a list of 13 subjects, but I think this will be the last. I wish to follow the theme expressed by the hon. member who just took his seat. If the task of the Minister of Finance and his official at this time in the economic history of Canada is to balance the budget, to get the country growing and expanding, the way it should be done is to take advantage of the evidence which is before the government, that is, tax rates in Canada today are not competitive with our main competitors. We can assume that is right without giving examples.
I have seen this growing over a number of years. The hon. member took advantage of that fact by mentioning the mineral industry. We developed a great mining industry in Canada by establishing a three-year tax exemption. This was to allow the mining industry time to pay off its debt and reduce its interest rate charges to a point where it could show some profit on its whole investment. Since that three-year exemption was removed, I have seen Canadian mining investment money move to other countries where they receive a higher return on their investment. The mining industry is one which is largely Canadian-owned.
I would like to give an example where this has taken place. Two of our largest industrialized types of companies, Algoma Steel and Steel Company of Canada in Hamilton, were engaged in a joint operation of developing what would have been the biggest iron mine in the world, north of Ignace, Ontario. In 1973 the provincial government got greedy and tripled the tax rate on large mines from 15 per cent to 45 per cent. Other provinces right through to the west coast did the same thing. In 1974 the federal government stepped in and in its two budgets of 1974 declared that provincial taxes and royalties were non-deductible. There was a 45 per cent tax by the province on a mining operation in a remote area north of Ignace, which is 200 miles from Thunder Bay, the federal government jumped in with a 42 per cent to 50 per cent tax rate, which was also non-deductible, then the effective tax load on that mining operation was over 90 per cent-45 per cent to the province and 42 to 50 per cent to the federal government, depending on the mine's income level. So those two large Canadian companies moved quietly across the border into Minnesota. They invested a billion dollars into developments of low-grade taconite, and today Canada imports raw iron from the United States. This puts Canadians out of work because of our tax laws.
Surely that is enough evidence in that one case alone, which affected the province of Ontario, where both the provincial government and the federal government in their quarrel and fight for revenues destroyed a very promising industry. This has all been admitted in the House. When the Hon. Don Macdonald was minister of finance he agreed this was so. He said we would have to obtain peace between the provinces and the federal government over this heavy taxation on resource industries.

February 2, 1981
Income Tax Act
At that particular time, when Mr. Tommy Douglas was in the House, the NDP were with the Conservatives asking for lower tax rates on resource industries. Now the NDP has allied themselves with this government. We have the two of them systematically driving industries out of this country. They then have the gall to turn around and complain that these companies in Ontario are importing iron from Minnesota, putting Canadians out of work. Who drove them out? This philosophy of driving taxes higher and higher to meet the demands of government drove two Canadian-owned, Canadian-controlled companies into development in high-priced ore in Minnesota. At least there they could make a profit out of their operations. But if they developed that iron ore in Canada they would lose money. I am simply saying the principle of reducing taxes to get more money is not only proven by quantitative analysis in almost every country in the western world, but it is clearly proven here in Canada where our tax rates are no longer competitive with the main competitors.
I want to conclude this series of hopefully constructive speeches on my part with how we can encourage Canadians to invest in their own country, to own their own companies in Canada as individuals and to make more money for the tax collector by investing in common shares. With present high interest rates all our large companies, in their fight for survival against these high interest rates, must shift from borrowing money at fixed rates to equity. Massey-Ferguson is putting out 30 million or 40 million new shares. Hopefully they can get rid of them. Stelco is moving into equity, as is Dofasco. In order to save themselves all our big companies must move into equity or they will be down the tube, just like the car companies. It is not only a question of bad management in borrowing money at these interest rates, but it is also a question of who it was who forced those interest rates up. It was a series of governments which did not measure on the basis of quantitative analysis of what was best, but on what the textbooks said one should do. Thus, we have this mad rush toward higher interest rates. The American nitwits, believing in the same rules and textbooks, are doing the same thing. This has been made clear by nearly everyone across this country, yet we have this determination to commit hara-kiri, suicide, or whatever one wants to call it, in the economic field. The very unique 1979 budget came out and gave a whole series of small examples on reducing taxation. One of them was on this question of encouraging Canadians to go into common stocks.
Of course, there will not be as much money in the beginning, but then there will not be a load on the company as it is developing. When the profits finally come the return from equity will be much bigger than the return from bonds. I would like to take the liberty of quoting for the record the proposal outlined in the 1979 budget which was defeated. I am quoting from page 11 of the budget papers, which reads as follows:
That for the 1980 and subsequent taxation years, a Canadian common stock investment plan for individual investors resident in Canada be introduced in respect of which the following rules will apply:
(a)	an investor may have only one plan at any time,
(b)	up to $20,000 may be contributed to the plan in 1980, thereafter annual contributions may not exceed $10,000 and total net contributions may not exceed $100,000,
(c)	the investments of the plan will be restricted to certain short-term debt obligations and to securities of taxable Canadian corporations that are common shares, warrants or rights in respect of such shares or shares that are convertible into common shares provided that such securities are listed on a prescribed stock exchange in Canada.
It goes on to say that dividends, interest and so on will be taxable. Every member of this House wishes to see-and the government has announced it as a priority-that Canada's resources are owned by Canadians. We know that these resources cannot be owned successfully by Crown corporations. We have the experience of the whole world and, indeed, of Canada to demonstrate that fact. The answer is to let millions of common Canadians invest in common stock, if 1 may use the word twice, so that they may own as individuals. As individuals who own investments in these companies, they will watch carefully and maintain the pressure to ensure that there is efficiency and growth within the company.
The omission from the present budget of that program, parts of which I just quoted, means the loss of a glorious opportunity for Canadians to own more of their country through buying individual shares. Of course, they would expect to receive a larger return later on than if they were to buy bonds. We have all learned over these past ten years that any person who buys a bond is cutting his financial throat and will lose his money because of inflation. But here is a way of fighting inflation, of putting more people to work, producing more goods and, thereby, more revenue for the government to help reduce our deficit. The government could then look for other ways to reduce taxes.
The question of common shares has been in my mind ever since I came to this House. If one looks at the regulations put forward in 1957 with regard to oil, gas and minerals in the north one will be proud, as I was. I waited for so long for Canadians to have the opportunity to own their own country as individuals, instead of our industry being owned primarily by people outside the country. For example, in the case of our oil the provincial government regulations turned our oil industry over to foreign companies. But on the Canada lands which were controlled by the federal government, Canadians would have the first chance to own and control the resources as well as receiving the bulk of the revenues. Those oil and gas regulations were brought up to date and improved in 1976 and supported by my party.
To see those regulations destroyed through the legislation which came before Parliament this year was simply cruel. All the advances toward the objective of Canadian ownership, which is the purpose of the government, were destroyed by that legislation. This debate has been going on for several days, and the government has been very good in allowing hon. members to speak their minds. Most of the members who have spoken have tried their level best to put forward positive suggestions.
February 2, 1981

There has been the suggestion that the government try to save the Small Business Development Bond. I know that it is too late to go back and put in a section with regard to common shares. The time factor is too great. I hope the Minister of Finance and the government supporters behind him will remind each other over the next few months, before the next budget in the spring, to put that proposal back into the budget. Then all those other devices of reducing taxes and producing more to obtain more money for the tax collector will help to fight inflation, balance the budget and get this country back in shape.
This is not my view alone. An election was fought in the United States last fall on this very issue, and everybody laughed. They said, "Imagine reducing taxes to make more money, how ridiculous". However, there is the precedent in the United States in 1963-1964, and there are many more as well.
The first minister of finance to ever introduce such a proposal was the hon. member for St. John's West. I was not here for the budget speech, as everyone knows. However, after reading the budget paper, I realized that this was a very unique budget. Even though the government was defeated on that budget, I went out and spoke at meetings throughout my constituency and, although I found great excitement over the fact that the government had been defeated, there was an awful lot of sadness because the things for which I had fought and which had appeared in small measure in the budget had been voted down.
People had no trouble in saying that his was a good budget, or, at least, not too bad. It distressed me to see the election fought on issues which had no relationship to the fact that here was the first budget in Canadian history which was attempting to balance the budget by reducing taxes. As I have mentioned in the House before, the intellectuals of the English-speaking world will soon be teaching their classses about this unique budget. Before long, that viewpoint will go throughout the entire populous and will ultimately come back to Canada. Everybody knows what I meant when 1 told the Minister of Finance some weeks ago that I felt sorry for him because he had an economic policy which was suposed to be as disciplined as the 1979 budget, that he zigged when he should have zagged.
I ask the government to consider the proposals put forward by several hon. members with regard to the Small Business Development Bond and to do some real thinking with regard to the matters of capital gains, energy tax credits, reducing taxes in resource industries to increase production, reducing the taxes on the movement of energy and reducing the taxes on the more value-added industries because of cheaper energy in Canada. There is lots of energy in this country, we are a strong country. Let us get it on the go. Let us not muck up this country with the stupid idea that we must keep raising taxes and making tax laws more complicated in the hope of receiving more money, because there will not be any more money if the taxes are too high. I suggest in all seriousness, because we will be in this House together for four years, that we begin with
Income Tax Act
this job right away or the opportunities which are before us now in this world of nations will be gone forever.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to endorse what the hon. member for Qu'appelle-Moose Mountain had to say about Canadian ownership of Canadian equity. Before becoming a Member of Parliament, 1 was involved for 20 years in the business community. 1 was president of a company which offered its common stock to the employees and encouraged them to buy it. No single action that company took in a period of 15 years was more positive and constructive to both the employees and the company than placing part of the ownership in the employees' hands. 1 might also say that there could be no more constructive force in the Canadian economy than placing equity in the hands of the Canadian people.
Just recently I returned from a visit to Sweden as a member of a task force which was investigating how Canada might improve trade with that country through a national trading corporation. Only a few years ago Sweden was held up as a model economy in the free world. I would urge all hon. members to go to Sweden today and see that model, that socialist experiment. It would be particularly interesting to my friends on my left.
In 1980 Sweden had a fiscal deficit of $18 billion. That is equivalent to a $50 billion fiscal deficit in Canada, yet Sweden has a population of only eight million people.
Do you know what you are talking about?

In Sweden, if you earn $25,000 per year, you pay $13,000 in taxes. That means your marginal rate of tax is 75 per cent. If you earn $32,000, the marginal rate of tax is 85 per cent. That is the social experiment, Mr. Chairman. While I was in Sweden there was a rather large snowfall so I had to buy a pair of galoshes. They cost me 159 kroner or $50 Canadian. I could have bought them here for under $10.
What Calgary interest are you representing?
The Swedes have nationalized the iron ore industry. They have nationalized the steel industry. They have nationalized their-
We have done that.
Does the hon. member want to listen or does he want to talk?
I would like to listen to some sense.

I thought it was my turn. Sweden has nationalized the steel industry, the coal industry and the shipbuilding industry. In 1970 their standard of living was the second highest in the free world; today it is twentieth. That is what the socialist experiment has done for Sweden.

They have had a Tory government for three years.

February 2, 1981
Income Tax Act
They have the highest suicide rate in the world and one of the highest rates of alcoholism. What has the socialist experiment done for Sweden?
Ruined it.
This brings me to the question: Is Canada going down the same road?
Oh, no!
Oh, yes!

No, Canada is not going down the same road! We are not living beyond our means! The Canadian government is not living beyond our means! We had no real growth in our country in 1980 and yet the level of government expenditures increased from $54 billion to $63.5 billion. In 1981-82 there will be a no-growth situation again, yet government expenditures will rise to $73.5 billion.
In 1980 the federal government took 25 per cent of the gross national product; in 1981-82 it intends to take 30 per cent of the gross national product.
What was it that caused Sweden to go downhill, Mr. Chairman? It happened because nobody cared enough to make the capital investment needed to create jobs. The government has taken so much money out of the economy that nothing was left with which to create capital investment. The same thing is happening in Canada. The Liberal government has made no effort whatsoever to restrain its expenditures.
Instead of focusing on growth and increasing the size of the economic pie, the Liberal government has focused on ways to take more and more revenue from the same size of pie and from a stagnating economy.
The Liberal government claims that it must have more revenue and that the revenue must come from the oil industry; that the oil industry is going to have to pay!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: That is what you wanted to do last year. The Canadian people would have paid.

The sad part of this is that any knowledgeable authority-and I would not expect to find any on the other side of the House-would say that we must spend between $400 and $600 billion in the next ten years if we are to have the energy which will be required to fuel our economy. Yet the Liberal government tells us that it is not going to give industry the money to do that; that it is going to take it away from industry. That means there is no hope of energy security for the Canadian people. That is the policy of this government.
The October, 1980, budget of the Minister of Finance was not concerned with fiscal policy; it was simply a statement of the National Energy Program. Surely the cornerstone of any energy policy should be the assurance of supply for Canadians. That surely should be the most important consideration for the next ten to 20 years. Instead, the National Energy Program is a plan to penalize industry and discourage investment when it should be seeking ways to improve production and to eliminate
the crude oil imports which in 1980 amounted to the staggering sum of $7.5 billion. It takes but a fraction of a second to say $7.5 billion, Mr. Chairman. But it is over 10 per cent of the gross spending of the federal government. It is 3 per cent of the gross national product. It is a staggering amount of money that does not need to be spent and that is the tragedy. Canada does not need to fork out $7.5 billion for imports when it could spend that money at home where it would create jobs and mean energy security for Canadians.
The worst part of this is the immorality of the government saying it is going to borrow $3 billion to subsidize the consumption of gasoline in this country, and that the Canadian people will assume that burden. That decision is immoral and there is no economic justification for it.
Assessments of the National Energy Program so far have indicated that the goal of self-sufficiency will not be reached by the end of this decade. Indeed, the National Energy Program itself will be a major hindrance to achieving this goal. How many people across Canada have said that time and time again? Is everybody in Canada out of step with the Liberal government and with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources? Is everybody in Canada out of step with them?
No, only the oil industry.
Who else? What about the Canadian Construction Association? What about the Canadian Manufacturers' Association?
How about Bill Davis?
What about the bankers? Are they out of step?
Tell us.
There is not much point, you do not listen.

The program is deficient on at least four major counts. First, the price of oil has not been increased sufficiently to promote conservation and to provide a return to the producer sufficient to promote exploration and development. Exploration capital is already leaving to seek higher returns elsewhere. Those are irrefutable facts.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The first one is easy to refute. Do you think people are dumb?
There are none so blind that will not see.
You should coin that phrase.
Second, the program is unrealistic in its treatment of western Canada. It fails to look upon the development of the west as a great opportunity for all Canadians.

Nonsense.
February 2, 1981
Nonsense? Go to Calgary, go to Edmonton, go to Estevan and see the rigs crossing the border. Watch the companies shutting down. For heaven's sake, open up your eyes.
He is afraid to.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are more there this year than there were last year.
You do not know what you are talking about.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Go easy. Listen to people.
Go out and take a look.

Third, the arbitrary and punitive thrust of the program makes it a focal point for forces that are attempting to divide the country.
Fourth, the program is a move to increase government involvement in the industry. This is a backward step. The oil and gas industry, as most industries, cannot be operated by government; governments cannot operate industry. Things are created and a country is built with entrepreneurial spirit whether or not hon. members want to believe it.
Adam Smith lives again.

The oil industry needs profit-orienting goals to produce continuing successful exploration and development.
Knowledgeable authorities throughout Canada have stated that the National Energy Program will leave Canada with substantially higher shortfalls in production in the 1980s, which will mean increased dependence on imported oil by 1985. Instead of seizing the opportunity for the oil and gas industry to make a substantial contribution to the economic growth of Canada, Canada's growth prospects under the National Energy Program are dismal, if not negative.
Some competent authorities have gone so far as to say the National Energy Program could be instrumental in producing a national economic disaster. At the core of the criticism of the National Energy Program is the issue of oil pricing and the attempt to isolate Canada from international energy markets.
The day after the Minister of Finance introduced his budget, 1 remember the headlines of the Economist in Britain. It read: "Canada resigns from the world." That is what we have done. Do you know of any other country in the industrialized free world which is pursuing the madness of energy prices at less than 50 per cent of world price, Mr. Chairman? Do you know of any other government in the world that is doing that? It is madness.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Is there any other country better than Canada?
Yes.

Canada must surely realize that this country is part of the world energy system. Do we not have to recognize that we are part of the world? Prices for petroleum will remain high. They will likely go higher. Given the relative-
Income Tax Act
ly short life of our remaining oil reserves, Canada cannot afford to subsidize the consumption of such a valuable resource. I ask the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare to tell me which country is subsidizing the consumption of a scarce resource? Is any other country in the industrialized world subsidizing the consumption of a scarce commodity?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Name a better country than Canada.
Alberta.
I would not name it. I love this country. That has nothing to do with the economic policies put forward by the hon. member's government.
Hear, hear!

Only when Canadians establish the price of their petroleum resources near the levels at which most world petroleum is bought and sold will rational decisions regarding the production and consumption of petroleum be made in Canada. Prices must be higher if we are to conserve our scarce resources and continue to search in Canada for new discoveries rather than looking in the United States or elsewhere.
Or Senegal.

Surely it makes sense to invest money in Canada rather than providing an incentive for companies to look abroad. Hon. members can laugh, but they will be laughing at the people who will be out of work as a result of the government's National Energy Program.
Apart from raising prices to achieve conservation, additional revenues received by the industry would encourage exploration. I could show hon. members case after case where the National Energy Program has had the effect of reducing producer netbacks to negative figures. In Saskatchewan and British Columbia it no longer pays to produce gas or oil from many fields. How can we possibly improve supply by making it uneconomic to produce and explore?
Higher oil prices now may ultimately be less expensive to Canada by speeding up energy resource development and reinforcing incentives toward conservation. The end result would be a reduced need for imports. Under the energy program the total burden of oil imports will eventually be borne through an additional tax on consumers of petroleum products, but in the interim taxpayers will continue to bear the burden of the rising costs of subsidies for oil imports. Reduced imports, therefore, would decrease government expenditures on subsidies. This would restore to the federal government some freedom of action in fiscal policy that a succession of federal deficits has taken away. A lower deficit with its reduced borrowing requirements would tend to reduce pressure on interest rates. I say to my friends on the left, "if you want lower interest rates, let us take a step in the right direction by reducing the federal deficit".
Borrowing requirements would tend to reduce the pressure on industry. The government would also have the option of

February 2, 1981
Income Tax Act
cutting some income taxes. Heaven forbid we should ever cut income taxes. Such reductions could be made in individual income taxes or in manufacturers' sales tax. It is likely that an increase in petroleum prices substantially offset by tax reductions would not exacerbate inflation. We are all concerned with inflation. In addition to these considerations, it must be remembered that the cost of not raising prices might be actual shortages of petroleum products in the future.
Every region of Canada can benefit from the development of oil and gas resources in the western provinces, off the east coast and in the Arctic. The further development of other energy sources throughout this nation, whether from hydroelectric power, nuclear power or renewable sources, will also stimulate national economic growth. In past years, major development projects such as the TransCanada PipeLine, the resources boom of the 1950s and others have given Canada strong impetus to economic growth and have strengthened our nation tremendously. Let us pursue energy developments of the eighties in the same way, as a source of economic strength, as a key to rapid economic growth and increased productivity and as a spur to greater political and economic unity.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to be nearly as long, and I do not intend to discuss Sweden. However, I do not mind pointing out there is no doubt that with the introduction of the policies of the Conservative government in Sweden after the defeat of the social democratic party three years ago, Sweden did go downhill rapidly.
He didn't know they had been defeated.

This not being the place to discuss that, I want to talk about conditions in Canada for a moment or two. I will deal with the matter I started to speak about on Friday last. Before I get to it, I want to raise with the minister, since we are talking about income tax, the tax rates paid by lower income earners in this country.
I was in Hamilton today to see constituents and to attend the funeral of a long time friend who served in the Ontario legislature for over 20 years. While there, a woman visited me in my constituency office in order to talk about problems that confront her. This woman, who works as a beauty parlour operator, earns approximately $6,000 a year. As she outlined her difficulties to me, it became very clear that on $6,000 one cannot afford to pay income tax.
This is a woman in her middle years, obviously independent and desirous of making her own way, not eager to become part of the statistics of government expense. She pointed out the rent she has to pay, her cost of food, which rises every day, her normal costs attached to living and her costs of going to work, providing uniforms and getting them cleaned. After adding up all those costs, what this woman really needed was the money she paid on income tax just to make ends meet.
The federal government should ask Alberta to give us a little of its oil money so that this poor woman will not have to pay
income tax out of such a meagre wage. I listened to the hon. member for Calgary South speak about how the system works and the fact that the oil companies are not getting enough money, how they need more and more, and how they are going to raise their prices in order to get even more, which is considerably in excess of what they can use. It makes me think of this woman in my office pointing out to me her fixed costs over which she has absolutely no control. I wonder just where our priority ought to lie.
If the minister has an opportunity to respond, I ask him to share with us his thoughts on undertaking a review of the income tax structure at the lowest levels, for a start. Possibly it could be substantiated that our cut-off point is too low. In keeping with the obvious need, we should consider whether there are ways to introduce a higher level of personal deduction or some form of rebate or credit which would afford these people an opportunity to meet their commitments on a day-today basis. They just cannot make it.
Knowing the minister's interest in the matter, it is not necessary to go into detail. However, it galls me when a member of this place talks about the billions of dollars going into the coffers of the multinational oil companies to be taken out of this country and invested elsewhere. I think of this woman who was born in Canada, lived here all her life, has worked every day since her mid-teens and cannot make ends meet. The hon. member is prepared to raise her costs. This woman's heating costs will go up so that the multinational oil companies can take her money to invest in some other part of the world. I find that a difficult argument to accept. It is time that members of this House who raise matters of this kind got out of this place and spoke to those who built this country and cannot afford to pay any more. We should take a serious look at the system which now exists.
I read a story over the weekend which brought this back to mind. It is in the justice column of the November 17 issue of Maclean's magazine. I commend it to the minister as there is a certain amount of value to be gleaned from it. The story, written by Ann Silversides is headed "The Catch-22 of single parents on welfare".
This article states almost exactly what I raised in the House on Friday last. It speaks of the entrapment of people within the system and how difficult it is for them to get out of it. With a family to raise, they must find a job. They discover that women in the work force earn just slightly more than 50 per cent of that earned by men. Therefore, they must raise their family on an income considerably less than is normally considered to be required in order to survive in this country. This article confirms what I said on Friday when speaking on another piece of legislation.
I do not want to repeat myself unnecessarily, but we are facing difficult times in this country. There are ever-larger numbers who have to raise their families alone. Within the income tax structure and grant structures which flow from the distribution of income, we must find a way to support these people during their difficult transitional period, at the same time encouraging them to upgrade or use their current skills in
February 2, 1981

order to fit into the work force. They should not have to choose between a job on one hand and welfare payments on the other. The vast majority would prefer to work. However, the income levels available to the majority of women are not enough to pay the bills. Unfortunately, because of the one-for-one ratio, if they accept a part-time job, they lose a dollar for every dollar they earn, placing them in a situation which deprives not only themselves, but their children. This interesting article refers to the problem of not being able to do for your kids what everybody else on the street is doing for theirs.
I just do not believe as I look at the billions and billions of dollars we spend and think of the tens of hundreds of billions of dollars we are projecting we will spend, and the fact that by and far the majority of that money, 99 per cent, will be raised in one way or another through the tax structure, that we cannot find a way here to undertake a meaningful review of the plight, first of the lady I spoke of whose income really does not afford her enough money to pay taxes, and of the people who, through no fault of their own in many cases, and in some cases perhaps even through a fault of their own, but who cares because it does not matter in the long run, are faced with poverty and with the problem of being trapped in a system which almost requires that they stay on social assistance. I know my good friend and colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West who is sitting listening with rapture to what 1 am saying, is very sympathetic to this because 1 am sure he deals with people in this category frequently on the weekends. I am sure if he has the opportunity he will be saying to the minister, either privately in his ear or publicly in the House of Commons, that we have reached that point in time where we have to review the structure of the tax system with which we live.
I know the minister remembers the Carter commission and the work done by Mr. Carter-1 cannot remember his name, who said that the whole tax structure has to be reviewed, we have to consider a dollar as a dollar; a buck is a buck is a buck and we must tax it that way. We cannot have different systems for different people. We cannot have a system in which the wealthier you are the less you pay in proportion because the more you can write off.
I think what we are seeing is Canada being bogged down by an inadequate non-progressive system. I should like to ask the minister whether he can explain to us at this point in time not only the content of this bill, which really in itself does not address this particular problem, but what kind of review is currently under way and what we can expect to see in the next two or three years before this Parliament is dissolved. I do not think this can go on much longer. It is not possible for this country to hold together, if we have such poverty at some levels and such wealth at others. I do not think we can argue with any degree of conviction for ever greater sums of money for the multinational oil companies, while at the other end of the scale we are completely ignoring the plight of so many Canadians who have worked all their lives but who, through no fault of their own are unable to earn sufficient to make ends
Income Tax Act
meet, expecting that somehow or another they will dig even deeper, tighten their belts, as the Prime Minister once said, do without something, change their priorities and continue to pay ever greater sums to people who in fact have more than they can use now. I would certainly appreciate it if the minister could take a moment now to perhaps explain this to us. Is he going to do it later; a lot later?
At the end of the debate.
You will not forget?
Indeed I will not.

This ir really important. It is probably more important than a discussion of Sweden's social structure. I have a sneaky suspicion we cannot do a lot about Sweden's social structure. 1 have a sneaky suspicion we cannot do anything about the financial problems of Sweden either, but I think we can do something about problems here. subtopic: HEALTH CARE-USE OF PRE-NATAL SCREENING KITS
HEALTH CARE-USE OF PRE-NATAL SCREENING KITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 18, 1980, I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) what steps her department was taking with respect to the sale and promotion of certain pre-natal screening kits, mainly, the Alpha-fetoprotein kits which are designed to detect the neurological disease called spinal bifida.
My concern arose out of the fact that the manufacturers of these kits were then beginning a hard promotion campaign with doctors and that there was and is a significant uncertainty about the accuracy of the kits. The minister responded in the House by saying that the problem was "misuse" of the kits "more than anything else" and that she had written to provincial health ministers warning them of the dangers of misuse.
This response is inadequate in itself in so far as the misuse as such is not the only problem. This glosses over the fact that the kits themselves and their questionable accuracy is also at issue. 1 am glad that to some extent the minister has gone beyond her answer on that point in the House and has forbidden the sale of these kits and has restricted their use to research and investigative purposes.
Nevertheless, the minister's response at that time and in a subsequent letter to me is inadequate in a larger sense, because it is another example of the way in which the Canadian testing and approval system for new medical devices is totally unacceptable and is desperately in need of improvement.
The department contends that the onus is on the manufacturer to prove the safety and efficiency of medical devices. That sounds good except that the manufacturer must only do so if requested by the department. The department usually asks after there has been controversy and the product has already been widely distributed, marketed and used by many Canadians. This is not the kind of pre-market testing that Canadians have a right to expect from the government; in fact, it takes place more often in the United States than it does in Canada. What we have in Canada is a kind of post-market system of testing which uses Canadian people as guinea pigs.
1 submit that we must no longer be content, and certainly many of us have never been content, although the government seems to have been for some time now, with a system that puts the onus on the Canadian people to get sick or die. It puts the onus on them until the medical device is proven unsafe.
The whole concept of the burden of proof in our society with respect to medical devices, with respect to new drugs, with respect to environmental questions of pollution, occupational health and safety, environmental health-the whole notion of
Adjournment Debate
the burden of proof must be transformed from that of putting the onus for proof on the victim to putting the onus for proof on the promoter of a particular product in the marketplace. Long-term tests of a particular product, for instance, must be done only with the informed consent of the people who participate in them. That is not an impractical proposal, Mr. Speaker. Officials of the department claim that people like me who complain about this are being ridiculous; that there are so many devices on the market that the department could hardly be expected to test them all.
The fact remains that only a very few of these devices, which fall into special categories, are tested at all. The Department of National Health and Welfare could find it within its budget, if it were motivated by a concern for the health and welfare of Canadian people, to increase the number of devices tested in this pre-market way that I have suggested and, as 1 requested in committee on one occasion, the department should do more to articulate the notion of burden of proof which would remove it from the Canadian consumer.
Finally, in the course of my work as NDP health critic, I have complained in this House on a number of occasions about the lack of adequate testing of certain products on the market which are related to health care. More often than not in my experience to this point, I have found that those products which eventually become a source of controversy and about which a great deal of concern develops, are products related to the health and welfare of Canadian women.
There are several things that I have had occasion to bring to the attention of the department. For instance, the question of toxic shock syndrome, because that sort of thing is not being researched. According to the department it was not a priority. Last year the contraceptive drug depo-provera was in question and as was the drug bendectin, a drug used by women. The list of things goes on and on about which there is a great deal of uncertainty in the minds of Canadian people. We seem to have no policy in which we can put some confidence.
Trying to get beyond the game of simply responding to questions that I raised in the House, I want to take this opportunity in the time left to me to urge upon the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Frith), and through him to the ministry of health, that it is about time the Canadian government started to take these kinds of problems seriously. It should stop the system by which the Canadian people themselves are bearing the burden of inadequate pre-market policies employed by the Ministry of National Health and Welfare.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: HEALTH CARE-USE OF PRE-NATAL SCREENING KITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two specific points which the hon. member has raised. One deals with some remarks he made toward the end of his comments which revolve around the use of drugs and how drugs marketed in Canada come to be allowed on the market.

February 2, 1981
Adjournment Debate
The record in Canada speaks for itself with respect to the safety record of the department concerning those drugs which are allowed on the market.
The hon. member's second point concerns medical devices. 1 can advise the hon. member that the minister instructed departmental officials in the fall of 1980, during the controversy over the toxic shock syndrome issue, to put more emphasis on the area of how medical devices are marketed in Canada.
When the issue was originally raised about the AFP test, 1 think the minister correctly pointed out in the House that her recommendation was that this was only one of the diagnostic choices available to physicians in this area of neuro-tube defects. The minister did point out how under specific conditions the test should be used. She further pointed out in the House at that time that she had instructed her provincial counterparts in a letter about the limitations of the use of the AFP test. She also suggested that competent AFP testing facilities should be developed under provincial jurisdiction.
With respect to the AFP tests, the minister also sent out a medical alert to physicians outlining the conditions by which AFP could be used as a diagnostic tool. She also instructed the department to come up with what we call a standard serum. In other words, the test itself could be compared to a purified
sample, which is available here in Ottawa, and provided to any of those designated testing centres.
However, the test itself has been banned in terms of its sale by the eight manufacturers on the kit. At present, they are only being used for research and investigative work. The manufacturers as well have instructed physicians about the proper use of the AFP kit. I am confident, with respect to AFP, that it is basically under control.
I want to emphasize a point I made earlier. When it comes to a device which is allowed on the market under the medical devices regulations, the minister instructed her department to put more emphasis on those products and the way in which they are marketed in Canada. Quite frankly, and I say this sincerely, knowing the pharmaceutical industry to the extent that 1 do, I think the department's record with respect to drugs allowed and marketed in the Canadian drug field is an excellent one. I would take some exception to what the hon. member says are some deficiencies when it comes to the marketing of drugs in this country. When it comes to drugs being allowed on the market we probably have the safest record of the western industrialized world.
